title: Sudan As A Mirror For Today’s World | NOEMA
gist: Historians Alden Young and Muez Ali argue that Sudan's war (14M+ internally displaced, 4.4M+ refugees since April 2023) is not post-American anarchy but a return to 19th-century political and trade patterns, as the colonial infrastructure (Gezira cotton, railways to Port Sudan, oil pipelines) that let the central state tax chokepoints decays along with the liberal order. Untaxable artisanal gold flowing via the RSF to Dubai, revived desert routes to Egypt and Libya, and RSF parallels to the merchant-warlord Zubayr Pasha illustrate why the 19th-century map is becoming a better model for post-liberal statecraft.

insights.claim: In the 2000s Sudan was a flagship laboratory for multilateral intervention: the US-UK-Norway troika mediated the end of the 1983-2005 civil war (2M+ dead), and two large UN missions (the 13-year AU-UN hybrid operation in Darfur ending 2020 and the six-year UN Mission in the Sudan ending 2011) culminated in South Sudan's independence.
insights.speaker: ALDEN YOUNG AND MUEZ ALI
insights.so_what: Benchmarks how much Western diplomatic capital has been withdrawn from African conflict management relative to two decades ago.
insights.quote: The level of Western concern and diplomatic resources mobilized to intervene in Sudan’s conflicts in the early 2000s feels almost unimaginable today.
insights.locator: At the time, finding a solution

insights.claim: The UN General Assembly's 2005 adoption of Responsibility to Protect, intellectually rooted in South Sudanese diplomat Francis Mading Deng's idea of 'sovereignty as responsibility', marked a high-water point for the legitimacy of the liberal world order.
insights.speaker: ALDEN YOUNG AND MUEZ ALI
insights.so_what: Frames the current non-intervention in Sudan as a reversal of the R2P norm, lowering the expected odds of external stabilization in fragile states.
insights.quote: marked a high-water point for the legitimacy of the liberal world order
insights.locator: It was in this context

insights.claim: Sudan has become a playground for a wide range of foreign actors across the Middle East and Africa, Russia and Ukraine, and even Colombia, while Trump administration cuts to USAID have weakened even the commitment to prevent famine.
insights.speaker: ALDEN YOUNG AND MUEZ ALI
insights.so_what: Aid retrenchment plus multipolar meddling means Sudan's humanitarian crisis is likely to persist and spill into neighboring states without a Western backstop.
insights.quote: After the Trump administration’s cuts to organizations like the U.S. Agency for International Development, even the commitment to prevent the spread of famine has declined.
insights.locator: In many ways, what is happening

insights.claim: Citing G. John Ikenberry, the authors note that the liberal international order's collective nature was always more aspirational than practical, with the United States acting since 1945 as its owner and operator; Sudan shows what happens when the US stops bearing that burden.
insights.speaker: ALDEN YOUNG AND MUEZ ALI
insights.so_what: Implies that order in peripheral regions was a US-subsidized public good; its withdrawal raises risk premia across fragile-state geographies.
insights.locator: The Fragile Liberal International Order

insights.claim: Since fighting between the SAF and RSF broke out in April 2023, at least 14 million Sudanese have been internally displaced and at least 4.4 million have fled abroad, largely to Chad, Egypt and South Sudan, which can ill afford the influx; three years on, fighting continues in Kordofan, Darfur and Blue Nile.
insights.speaker: ALDEN YOUNG AND MUEZ ALI
insights.so_what: Refugee burdens on already fragile neighbors (Chad, Egypt, South Sudan) are a regional destabilization vector worth tracking.
insights.quote: At least 14 million people have been internally displaced since the latest round of fighting in April 2023, according to the United Nations Refugee Agency.
insights.locator: Today, the conflict in Sudan

insights.claim: The authors describe the Sudan conflict as a world war in microcosm, given the number of external actors involved and the scale of destruction.
insights.speaker: ALDEN YOUNG AND MUEZ ALI
insights.so_what: Sudan should be read as a proxy arena for Gulf, Russian and African rivalries rather than a contained civil war.
insights.quote: Today, the conflict in Sudan can be described as a world war in microcosm.
insights.locator: Today, the conflict in Sudan

insights.claim: Contrary to Anne Applebaum's view that Sudan shows a nihilistic, anarchic post-American world where the liberal order has ended with nothing to replace it, the authors argue the war reveals a return to precolonial political and trade patterns.
insights.speaker: ALDEN YOUNG AND MUEZ ALI
insights.so_what: If disorder is patterned, outcomes (which routes, actors and enclaves dominate) become forecastable using historical maps rather than treated as random chaos.
insights.quote: But what is taking place in Sudan and elsewhere is not the emergence of anarchy; it is a return to precolonial patterns.
insights.locator: But what is taking place in Sudan

insights.claim: Observers misread the region because of what historian Richard Reid calls the 'foreshortening of African history', detaching Africa's turbulent present from deeper patterns of change and continuity; post-colonial chaos is not the product of ethnic rivalries.
insights.speaker: ALDEN YOUNG AND MUEZ ALI
insights.so_what: Challenges ethnic-conflict risk models; analysts should weight trade-route and infrastructure geography over ethnic maps.
insights.quote: Just as the chaos marring the post-colonial period is not a result of ethnic rivalries.
insights.locator: A Return To The Pre-Colonial Era

insights.claim: The breakdown of the Sudanese state is not random: older orders reappear because they rest on trade and political-economic linkages that do not depend on colonial-era infrastructure, whose durability has decayed as the liberal-order institutions maintaining it crumbled.
insights.speaker: ALDEN YOUNG AND MUEZ ALI
insights.so_what: Infrastructure-anchored state power is reversible; investors in fragile states should not assume colonial-era trade corridors persist.
insights.quote: These patterns repeat because they are based on trade and political and economic linkages that do not rely on the infrastructure built during the colonial period.
insights.locator: The breakdown of the Sudanese state

insights.claim: The endurance of the colonial and postcolonial state in Sudan stemmed not from the destruction of African societies but from the legacy of its physical infrastructure.
insights.speaker: ALDEN YOUNG AND MUEZ ALI
insights.so_what: Central-state capacity in such economies is a function of infrastructure chokepoints; damage to them translates directly into fiscal collapse.
insights.quote: Rather, the endurance of colonialism in countries like Sudan is a product of the legacies of its infrastructure.
insights.locator: A Return To The Pre-Colonial Era

insights.claim: Drawing on Timothy Mitchell's 'The Alibi of Capital', the authors frame large infrastructure as a political technology for discounting and colonizing the future, whose durability depends as much on arrangements of law, authority and compulsion as on steel and concrete.
insights.speaker: ALDEN YOUNG AND MUEZ ALI
insights.so_what: Long-dated infrastructure assets carry political-order risk: when the authority arrangements behind them dissolve, their economic value can collapse.
insights.quote: depended not just on material durability but upon the durable arrangements of law, authority, compulsion, and justification
insights.locator: The peculiar durability of the infrastructure

insights.claim: The Gezira irrigation scheme, planned in the 1920s to irrigate more than a million acres as a cotton farm for the British Empire, oriented Sudan's railways, dams, ports, labor force and financial system until it hit financial trouble in the 1970s.
insights.speaker: ALDEN YOUNG AND MUEZ ALI
insights.so_what: Shows how a single export project can hardwire a country's entire economic geography for half a century.
insights.quote: was originally planned in the 1920s to irrigate more than a million acres
insights.locator: Sudan, though often imagined as a colonial backwater

insights.claim: Even after oil rose to prominence in the 1990s, pipelines and refineries followed colonial-era patterns, and Sudan integrated into global finance via export-backed loans tied successively to cotton, crude oil and now gold.
insights.speaker: ALDEN YOUNG AND MUEZ ALI
insights.so_what: Sudan's sovereign creditworthiness has always been commodity-collateralized; the shift to gold removes the state-controlled collateral base.
insights.quote: Originally, it was cotton, later crude oil and now gold.
insights.locator: This changed in the 1990s

insights.claim: For decades after 1956 independence, economic activity flowed from the provinces to Khartoum and then by rail to Port Sudan, and the government earned most of its revenue by taxing trade along this route; the RSF, holding Khartoum in the first two years of war, worked to break it.
insights.speaker: ALDEN YOUNG AND MUEZ ALI
insights.so_what: Severing the single taxable corridor is a deliberate fiscal-warfare strategy that starves the central state.
insights.quote: The government earned most of its revenue by taxing the imports and exports that followed this well-trodden route.
insights.locator: Precolonial Patterns Return In Contemporary Guises

insights.claim: Unlike cotton and crude oil, whose exports the central state could control directly or via licenses to favored clients, Sudan's gold export boom since 2013 has escaped state control, so the state missed the windfall from an almost 200% rise in gold prices over the period.
insights.speaker: ALDEN YOUNG AND MUEZ ALI
insights.so_what: Higher gold prices finance non-state armed actors rather than sovereigns in fragile producers, an under-appreciated second-order effect of the gold bull market.
insights.quote: the tragedy is magnified by the almost 200% rise in gold prices during that period
insights.locator: But what if what looks like chaos

insights.claim: Artisanal gold mining lacks the central infrastructural chokepoints (oilfields, pipelines, irrigation) that the colonial and postcolonial state had learned to tax, structurally undermining fiscal capacity.
insights.speaker: ALDEN YOUNG AND MUEZ ALI
insights.so_what: Commodity type determines state capacity: decentralized, portable resources favor militias and merchant networks over central governments.
insights.quote: artisanal gold production, unlike control of oilfields and pipelines or cotton irrigation, lacks the central infrastructural chokepoints
insights.locator: But what if what looks like chaos

insights.claim: A regional collapse of the taboo against dealing with subnational actors means Darfur gold reaches Dubai's souks without passing through the central government, and Sudanese soldiers guarding the Saudi-Yemeni border can be hired without contracting with the SAF.
insights.speaker: ALDEN YOUNG AND MUEZ ALI
insights.so_what: Gulf states transacting directly with militias normalizes sub-state sovereignty, eroding the value of recognized governments as counterparties.
insights.quote: gold from the mines of Darfur often ends up in the souks of Dubai without ever passing through the central government
insights.locator: The other dilemma for the Sudanese state

insights.claim: The RSF operates as a paramilitary-merchant company that executes these gold and mercenary transactions and manages large portions of Sudan on behalf of its investors.
insights.speaker: ALDEN YOUNG AND MUEZ ALI
insights.so_what: The RSF should be analyzed as a commercial enterprise with external investors, implying its behavior follows revenue routes rather than ideology.
insights.quote: The RSF, a paramilitary-slash-merchant company, carries out many of these transactions, managing large portions of Sudan on behalf of its investors.
insights.locator: The other dilemma for the Sudanese state

insights.claim: With the SAF holding Port Sudan, the RSF turned to old desert trade routes, including the Darb El Arba'in ('40 Day Road') from northern Darfur to Asyut in Egypt, routes into Libya under Khalifa Haftar's protection, and reactivated routes via South Sudan ending in Uganda, Kenya and the Central African Republic.
insights.speaker: ALDEN YOUNG AND MUEZ ALI
insights.so_what: RSF supply lines run through Libya and East Africa, making Haftar and neighboring states key leverage points for any settlement.
insights.quote: the RSF is suspected to have established bases under the protection of the Libyan militia leader who rules the eastern part of the country, Khalifa Haftar
insights.locator: But perhaps more dramatically, the war

insights.claim: The government's retreat to Port Sudan after Khartoum fell in 2023 echoed 19th-century Suakin and other Red Sea ports, which pledged allegiance to the Ottomans and sought incorporation into the Hijaz or Aden rather than into inland Sudanese kingdoms.
insights.speaker: ALDEN YOUNG AND MUEZ ALI
insights.so_what: Hints at latent risk of the Red Sea coast drifting into an Arabian-peninsula orbit, relevant to Red Sea shipping and Gulf basing competition.
insights.locator: Inadvertently, the war revealed older patterns

insights.claim: In April 2025, two years after the war began, the TASIS (Sudan Founding Alliance) declared a rival government from Nairobi, seeking to bind the RSF, part of the SPLM-N and the leadership of the Baggara confederation, which spans more than six million people from southern Kordofan to Lake Chad.
insights.speaker: ALDEN YOUNG AND MUEZ ALI
insights.so_what: A formalized parallel government hosted in Kenya raises the probability of a de facto partition of Sudan.
insights.quote: The Baggara includes more than six million Arab and African people stretching from southern Kordofan to Lake Chad.
insights.locator: The new prominence of the old trade routes

insights.claim: The RSF, founded in 2013 around the Darfurian Arab family of Muhammad Hamdan Daglo Musa, echoes Zubayr Pasha's 19th-century private-merchant empire, which grew into a quasi-independent state with some 12,000 soldiers and conquered the Fur Sultanate at El Fasher in 1874; the RSF likewise took El Fasher in late October 2025 after months of siege.
insights.speaker: ALDEN YOUNG AND MUEZ ALI
insights.so_what: Historical precedent suggests merchant-militias can become recognized governing authorities, as Egypt made Zubayr a governor after he defeated its force.
insights.quote: the RSF captured the last major stronghold in Darfur and solidified their ability to resupply to the north through Libya and to the south across the expanse of South Sudan into East Africa
insights.locator: Initially, Zubayr’s base was in the southern

insights.claim: Kordofan has re-emerged as a contested region as it was after Muhammad Ali's 1821 invasion from Egypt, with cities like El-Obeid (population over 600,000) under frequent attack as rival forces vie for control.
insights.speaker: ALDEN YOUNG AND MUEZ ALI
insights.so_what: Kordofan is the likely frontline of any partition, determining connectivity between RSF-held west and SAF-held east.
insights.quote: cities like El-Obeid, with a population over 600,000, remain under frequent attack
insights.locator: Yet another echo of the 19th century

insights.claim: SPLM-N factions sit on both sides of the war (Al-Hilu in the Nuba Mountains with the RSF, Agar in Blue Nile with the SAF), preserving borderland autonomy in a strategy the authors' Bergen archive research links to the Kingdom of Taqali, which pledged vassalage to both Darfur and Sennar simultaneously.
insights.speaker: ALDEN YOUNG AND MUEZ ALI
insights.so_what: Borderland actors hedging across both camps are likely to persist regardless of which side wins, complicating any centralized peace deal.
insights.quote: pledging vassalage to both simultaneously as they worked to maintain autonomy
insights.locator: Our research in the Sudan Collection

insights.claim: Sudan is one case of a wider pattern: re-emerging Trans-Saharan, East/Central African and Sahel-Red Sea routes, calls in South Africa to dissolve the 1910 Union, Yemen's decade-long redivision, and Russian aggression questioning eastern Europe's borders.
insights.speaker: ALDEN YOUNG AND MUEZ ALI
insights.so_what: Border and sovereignty stability that underpinned 20th-century country-risk assumptions should no longer be priced as a given.
insights.quote: the stability that defined the second half of the 20th century cannot be taken for granted
insights.locator: These are just a few examples

insights.claim: The authors predict that the 19th-century map of political competition and shifting boundaries will increasingly be the best model for understanding statecraft after the liberal order.
insights.speaker: ALDEN YOUNG AND MUEZ ALI
insights.so_what: Suggests geopolitical scenario analysis should use pre-colonial trade routes and polities as priors for where new power centers form.
insights.quote: it increasingly makes sense to look at the 19th-century map as an example of political competition and shifting boundaries
insights.locator: These are just a few examples
